outline.chapter_title: Introduction to Tabular Learning and Its Challenges
outline.description: Sets the stage by explaining why tabular data is ubiquitous in real‑world applications, the difficulty of learning from few labeled examples, and the limitations of conventional machine‑learning pipelines in low‑shot regimes.
subtopics: Definition and examples of tabular datasets
Typical supervised learning workflow for tabular data
Why few‑shot learning is needed (label cost, privacy)
Failure modes of standard models with limited data (over‑fitting, spurious correlations)
Motivation for leveraging external knowledge sources

outline.chapter_title: Large Language Models (LLMs) as General‑Purpose Reasoners
outline.description: Provides a concise yet complete background on modern LLMs—architecture, pre‑training on massive text corpora, emergent abilities such as in‑context learning—and why these properties make them attractive for tabular tasks.
subtopics: Pre‑training objectives (next token prediction) and knowledge acquisition
In‑context learning vs fine‑tuning vs parameter‑efficient tuning
APIs vs open‑source checkpoints: practical implications

outline.chapter_title: Few‑Shot Learning for Tabular Data: Prior Work
outline.description: Reviews existing strategies that combine tabular learning with auxiliary data or models—unsupervised pre‑training, self‑supervised augmentations, transfer across tables—and recent language‑interfaced approaches that use LLMs directly for prediction.
subtopics: Language‑interfaced methods: TabLLM, TABLET, In‑context tabular learners
Key limitations of prior LLM‑based approaches (per‑sample inference cost, prompt length constraints)

outline.(description):
"FeatLLM" shifts the role of an LLM from an end‑to‑end predictor to a rule generator that creates high‑quality binary features which can be used by a simple downstream classifier.
The chapter introduces the core idea and debates its benefits over previous paradigms.
(subtopics): "Why generate features instead of predictions?"
"Human expert analogy: extracting decision rules from data"
"Overview of the two-stage pipeline (rule extraction → feature construction → lightweight model)"
"Implications for inference latency and API usage"
"High‑level comparison table summarizing differences with TabLLM / TABLET

outline.(description): Formalizes the supervised classification setting used throughout the book; defines notation for raw tabular inputs, natural‑language feature descriptors, few‑shot subsets, and the target output space.
(subtopics):
$N$, $d$, $k$-shot setup\n\n---
$\mathbf{x}^i$, $\mathbf{y}^i$ definitions
Feature name set $F$ and optional definitions
Class set $\mathcal{C}$
Training/test split conventions used in experiments
Goal: learn a mapping $\mathbf{x}\mapsto \mathbf{p}$ using only $k$ labeled rows plus an LLM

outline.(description):
Explains how to craft effective prompts that coax the LLM into producing high‑quality decision rules.
Covers each component of the prompt—basic information block, reasoning instruction block, response instruction block—and provides design rationales.
(subtopics):
"Basic information description": task statement,
feature names + type/definition,
few‐shot examples serialization
"Reasoning instruction": two–step chain‑of‑thought (causal inference → rule synthesis)
"Response instruction": structured output format (JSON / bullet list), handling logical operators
Best practices for controlling temperature & max tokens
Example prompts (with annotated colors) reproduced from the paper

outline.(chapter_title): Two-Step Reasoning: From Causal Insight to Class Rules
outline.(description):
Details the internal reasoning phases enforced by the prompt.
Phase 1 extracts generic relationships between features and the task using LLM world knowledge.
Phase 2 uses few‐shot examples to ground those relationships into concrete decision rules per class.
(subtopics):
"Phase 1 – Knowledge mining": leveraging prior knowledge without looking at examples
Techniques to avoid spurious correlations
"Phase 2 – Rule synthesis": mapping example patterns onto conditions
Fixed number of rules per class (why 10?)
Handling categorical vs numeric features
Dealing with ambiguous or contradictory rules

outline.(chapter_title): Parsing Natural Language Rules into Executable Binary Features
(subtopics):
"Why parsing is nontrivial": noisy phrasing (e.g., ‘greater than’ vs ‘>’) , logical nesting
"Self‑parsing via LLM": feeding rule text back into LLM with a code generation prompt
Design of the parsing prompt (function signature, input/output description)
Executing generated Python code safely using `exec()`
Fallback strategies when parsing fails (rule filtering / requery)
Complexity analysis of rule‐to‐feature conversion

outline.(chapter_title): Learning from Generated Binary Features – Linear Model & Weight Tuning
outline.(description):
After rules are turned into binary columns $\mathbf{z}_k$, this chapter describes how a tiny linear model learns to weight each rule.
It also explains why nonnegative weights are enforced and how cross entropy training works with few shots.
(subtopics):
"Binary feature matrix construction" per class ($R$ rules each)
"Linear model without bias": $\text{logit}_k = \max(\mathbf{w}_k ,0) \cdot \mathbf{z}_k$
Softmax conversion to class probabilities
Training objective (cross entropy) with Adam optimizer
Hyperparameters for low‐shot training (learning rate,
epoch selection via cross validation)
Interpretability aspect: learned weights indicate rule importance

outline.(chapter_title): Ensembling via Bagging and Model Averaging
outline.(description):
Because each LLM query yields a stochastic set of rules (temperature > 0), we repeat rule generation many times.
Bagging selects random subsets of features / samples per trial to keep prompts short.
Ensemble predictions are averaged across $T$ trials.
The chapter formalizes bagging strategy and shows its dual benefits—robustness to noisy rules and mitigation of prompt length limits.
(subtopics):
"Stochasticity sources": temperature sampling,
demo order randomization
Bagging procedure – selecting $m$ features / $k$ examples per trial
Ensemble aggregation formula (average softmax probabilities)
Effect on variance reduction & bias–variance tradeoff
Practical guidance on choosing $T$ (e.g., 20) and bag size

outline.(description):
A systematic walk through the empirical section of the paper.
Describes each benchmark dataset (size,
type distribution), why they were chosen (including recent UCI additions),
and how they test different aspects such as feature count or domain novelty.
Summarizes all baseline families and reports main performance tables.
Highlights key takeaways:
* FeatLLM consistently top/second performer,
* matches 32-shot baselines with only 4 shots,
* robust under many features where other LLM methods fail.
(subtopics):
"Dataset catalogue": Adult, Bank,... ,Solution-mix etc., with brief domain description
"Baseline groups": conventional ML (LogReg/XGBoost/RandomForest), unsupervised/semi-supervised (SCARF/STUNT/TabPFN), LLM based (In-context,/TABLET/TabLLM)
Experimental protocol – $k$-shot values used,
cross validation splits,
evaluation metric (AUROC)
Result tables analysis – average AUC improvements (+10% over alternatives)
Effect of bagging on large–feature datasets

outline.(description):
Dissects the contributions of FeatLLM components through controlled ablations.
Also includes runtime comparison, feature quality assessment using AUROC per generated rule,
and robustness tests against spurious correlated columns.
(subtopics):
"Component ablations": -Tuning , -Ensemble , -Description , -Reasoning
Quantitative impact on AUC across datasets
Interpretation: why weight tuning matters more with more shots;
how reasoning instruction stabilizes performance in ultra low-shot regimes
Training vs inference time breakdown vs other LLM baselines
Feature quality metric: ratio of rules with AUROC > 0.5 before/after weight tuning
Spurious correlation experiment on Heart dataset – performance degradation curves
Discussion of failure cases where irrelevant but related columns still corrupt rules

outline.(description):
Guides practitioners through real-world deployment aspects such as API budgeting,
prompt length handling Strategies for large tables,
safety when executing generated code,
and integration pipelines for downstream systems.
(subtopics):
"API usage economics": number of calls per training run,
cost estimation for GPT-3.5 turbo;
batch parallelism options
Prompt size limits (≤ 8192 tokens) & mitigation via feature bagging
Robust parsing safeguards against malicious code injection
Deployable inference architecture:
   • offline rule generation phase → binary feature extractor → lightweight linear scorer
Latency comparison table vs end-to-end LLM inference
Guidelines for choosing an alternative backbone model (Claude, Gemini)

outline.(description):
Explores how FeatLLM could be expanded beyond binary rule features—e.g., generating richer transformations or embeddings—while preserving interpretability.
Discusses current constraints such as reliance on well-described feature names,
categorical explosion handling,
and potential bias amplification from LLM priors.
Outlines research avenues: scaling to larger labeled sets,
multi-task meta-learning using shared rule vocabularies,
and hybrid approaches combining tree ensembles with LLM-generated features.
(subtopics):
"Beyond rules": arithmetic expressions,
deep feature synthesis via program synthesis
"Scalability", handling millions of rows or thousands of columns
"Bias & fairness": probing how pretrained knowledge influences extracted criteria
"Hybrid pipelines": feeding FeatLLM features into gradient boosted trees or neural nets

"Open challenges", reproducibility across closed API models,
and evaluation on hidden testbeds

outline.(description):
Collects supplementary material useful for students who wish to reproduce experiments or extend the method.
Includes full prompt templates in both LaTeX and plain text form,
a brief tutorial on using OpenAI’s Python client for batch queries,
a checklist for debugging rule parsing errors,
and pointers to the public GitHub repository.
(subtopics): "Complete prompt listings" for basic info / reasoning / response sections
"Parsing prompt + example generated Python routine", "Error handling strategies"

"Reproducibility checklist": seed settings,
data splits properties
"Code repository overview", "Running experiments on new datasets"

"Further reading list": seminal papers on chain-of-thought prompting,
language-interfaced tabular learning
